title: LAG and LEAD Function in Oracle: Examples With Output
description: Learn the LAG and LEAD function in Oracle with runnable examples: previous row, next row, PARTITION BY, defaults, IGNORE NULLS and month-over-month change.
focusKeyword: lag and lead function in oracle

reviewNotes: All examples written from the Oracle 19c docs and not run; please test on 19c or later. Check: (1) the syntax block. The docs show the syntax only as a diagram; the article uses the form with IGNORE NULLS after the parentheses, matching the docs text. (2) The ORA-30483 wording 'window functions are not allowed here' came from Oracle Support note titles; confirm it on a real run of the WHERE example. (3) The expected outputs and date gaps were worked out by hand (2026 is not a leap year): 15/25/44 days for customer 1, 23/75 for customer 2, month totals 4500/4000/1350/3100. ROUND(-66.25,1) is expected to show -66.3. (4) The performance claims (WINDOW SORT, index may avoid the sort) are kept general on purpose; confirm the plan wording if you add a plan example. (5) NULL cells in the output tables are left blank, the way SQL*Plus shows them.

data.text: The LAG and LEAD functions in Oracle let you read a value from another row of the same result set without a self join. LAG looks back to an earlier row, LEAD looks ahead to a later row, and the ORDER BY inside OVER decides what "earlier" and "later" mean.

You use them to compare each row with its neighbour: the change from the previous order, the days until the next order, month-over-month growth, or the last known value when data has gaps. This tutorial walks through each case on a small orders table, with the expected output after every query.
How LAG and LEAD work

Both are analytic functions. Oracle first builds the result set (joins, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING), then sorts the rows as the OVER clause says, and then, for every row, reaches a fixed number of rows backwards (LAG) or forwards (LEAD) and returns a value from that row.

data.code:
LAG  ( value_expr [, offset [, default ]] )
     [ RESPECT NULLS | IGNORE NULLS ]
     OVER ( [ PARTITION BY expr, ... ] ORDER BY expr, ... )

LEAD ( value_expr [, offset [, default ]] )
     [ RESPECT NULLS | IGNORE NULLS ]
     OVER ( [ PARTITION BY expr, ... ] ORDER BY expr, ... )
data.caption: Syntax (Oracle 19c SQL Language Reference)

content: The column or expression to read from the other row. It cannot be another analytic function.
How many rows back (LAG) or forward (LEAD). An integer greater than zero.
Value returned when the offset goes past the start or end of the partition.
Whether rows where value_expr is NULL are counted when stepping back or forward.
Splits rows into groups. LAG and LEAD never cross a group boundary.
Whole result set is one group
Defines the row order inside each group. This is what makes "previous" meaningful.

data.text: The two functions are mirror images. LAG(amount) on a row gives the amount of the row before it; LEAD(amount) gives the amount of the row after it. Before these functions existed, the same result needed a self join on a row number, which is harder to read and usually slower.
Sample setup
Create this small table and run the inserts so you can follow every example. The dates are set so the gaps between orders are easy to check by hand.

data.caption: Sample orders table

data.text: LAG example: compare each order with the previous one
Start with one customer. For each order you want the previous order amount and the change from it.

data.code:
SELECT order_id,
       order_date,
       amount,
       LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)          AS prev_amount,
       amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS change
  FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id = 1
 ORDER BY order_date;
data.caption: Previous order amount for customer 1

data.text: Output (expected output). The first order has no earlier row, so LAG returns NULL and the change is NULL too. Every other row shows the amount of the order placed just before it. The WHERE clause runs before LAG, so only customer 1's rows take part.
LEAD example: days until the next order
LEAD works the same way in the other direction. Subtracting one DATE from another in Oracle gives a number of days, so you can measure the gap to the next order directly.

data.code:
SELECT order_id,
       order_date,
       LEAD(order_date) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)              AS next_order_date,
       LEAD(order_date) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) - order_date AS days_to_next
  FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id = 1
 ORDER BY order_date;
data.caption: Next order date for customer 1

data.text: Output (expected output). This time the last row is the one with no neighbour, so it gets NULL. If you only need days between orders, LAG and LEAD give the same gaps, just attached to different rows: LEAD puts the gap on the earlier order, LAG puts it on the later one.
If order_date were a TIMESTAMP instead of a DATE, the subtraction would return an INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND, not a number. Use CAST(... AS DATE) or EXTRACT(DAY FROM ...) if you need a plain number.
LAG with PARTITION BY: one result per customer

Real queries cover many customers at once. Add PARTITION BY customer_id so each customer is a separate group. LAG then restarts at the first order of every customer instead of reading another customer's order.

data.code:
SELECT customer_id,
       order_id,
       order_date,
       amount,
       LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                         ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS prev_amount
  FROM orders
 ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
data.caption: Previous order amount per customer

data.text: Output (expected output). Each customer's first order gets NULL, which is exactly what you want: a first order has no previous order. Customer 3 has only one order, so its only row is NULL. order_id is added to the ORDER BY as a tie-breaker, so if a customer ever places two orders on the same date the result is still predictable.
Offset and default value
The second argument sets how far to look, and the third sets what to return when there is no row that far away.
Step 1: look two rows back

data.code:
SELECT order_id,
       amount,
       LAG(amount, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_or_zero,
       LAG(amount, 2)    OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS two_back
  FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id = 2
 ORDER BY order_date;
data.caption: Offset 2 and default 0 for customer 2

data.text: Output (expected output). PREV_OR_ZERO uses offset 1 with default 0, so the first row shows 0 instead of NULL. TWO_BACK uses offset 2 with no default: the first two rows have nothing two places back and return NULL, and order 107 reads order 105.
Step 2: default is not the same as NVL

The default only applies when the offset points outside the partition. If the earlier row exists but its value is NULL, LAG returns that NULL, not the default. NVL(LAG(amount), 0) replaces both cases. Pick the one that matches what you mean. Also keep the default the same data type as value_expr, for example a date default for a date column, to avoid implicit conversion surprises.
IGNORE NULLS: get the previous non-null value

A common reporting problem is a series with gaps, where you want to carry the last known value forward. IGNORE NULLS makes LAG skip rows whose value is NULL and keep stepping back until it finds a real value.

data.caption: Sample table with missing prices

data.code:
SELECT price_date,
       price,
       LAG(price) OVER (ORDER BY price_date)              AS prev_respect,
       LAG(price) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY price_date) AS prev_ignore,
       NVL(price,
           LAG(price) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY price_date)) AS filled_price
  FROM price_history
 ORDER BY price_date;
data.caption: RESPECT NULLS vs IGNORE NULLS

data.text: Output (expected output). Look at 3 June. With the default RESPECT NULLS, LAG reads 2 June, which is NULL. With IGNORE NULLS, LAG skips 2 June and returns 100 from 1 June. FILLED_PRICE keeps a real price when there is one and falls back to the last known price when there is not.
LAST_VALUE(price) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY price_date) gives a similar fill-forward result. The difference is that it includes the current row, so you do not need the NVL wrapper.
Filter on LAG or LEAD results
Analytic functions are calculated after WHERE, so you cannot filter on them in the same query level. Compute them in an inline view and filter in the outer query.
Orders where the amount dropped

data.code:
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, amount, prev_amount
  FROM (SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, amount,
               LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                                 ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS prev_amount
          FROM orders)
 WHERE amount < prev_amount
 ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
data.caption: Orders smaller than the customer's previous order

data.text: Output (expected output). Order 106 is not listed because 2500 is equal to the previous amount, not lower. First orders drop out on their own, because amount < NULL is never true.
Customers who waited more than 30 days

data.code:
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, days_since_prev
  FROM (SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
               order_date - LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                                                  ORDER BY order_date, order_id)
                 AS days_since_prev
          FROM orders)
 WHERE days_since_prev > 30
 ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
data.caption: Gaps longer than 30 days between orders

data.text: Output (expected output). Customer 2 went 75 days between 2 February and 18 April. This is a typical churn or re-engagement check, and it needs no self join.
Month-over-month change with LAG and GROUP BY
LAG can read an aggregate. In a GROUP BY query, Oracle groups first and then applies the analytic function to the grouped rows, so LAG(SUM(amount)) gives the previous month's total.

data.code:
SELECT order_month, total, prev_total,
       ROUND((total - prev_total) * 100 / NULLIF(prev_total, 0), 1) AS pct_change
  FROM (SELECT TO_CHAR(TRUNC(order_date, 'MM'), 'YYYY-MM') AS order_month,
               SUM(amount) AS total,
               LAG(SUM(amount)) OVER (ORDER BY TRUNC(order_date, 'MM')) AS prev_total
          FROM orders
         GROUP BY TRUNC(order_date, 'MM'))
 ORDER BY order_month;
data.caption: Monthly totals and change from the previous month

data.text: Output (expected output). January has no earlier month, so its change is NULL. NULLIF(prev_total, 0) protects you from a divide-by-zero error if a month ever totals zero.

LAG returns the previous row, not the previous calendar month. If a month has no orders at all, it is missing from the grouped result, and the next month is compared with the month before the gap. When that matters, generate the full list of months first and outer join your totals to it.
Common mistakes
1. Forgetting PARTITION BY

Without PARTITION BY customer_id, the whole table is one group. With OVER (ORDER BY customer_id, order_date), order 105, the first order of customer 2, would show 900 as its previous amount, which is customer 1's last order. The numbers look plausible, which is why this bug survives testing. Partition by whatever defines "the same thing" in your question.
2. Putting LAG in the WHERE clause

data.code:
-- Fails: analytic functions are not allowed in WHERE
SELECT order_id, amount
  FROM orders
 WHERE amount < LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date);
data.caption: Wrong

data.text: Oracle rejects this with ORA-30483: window functions are not allowed here. Analytic functions can appear only in the select list or the ORDER BY clause. Use an inline view, as in the filtering section above.
3. An ORDER BY that has ties

If two rows have the same order_date within a customer, Oracle can return them in either order, and LAG may pick a different "previous" row on different runs. Add a unique column, such as order_id, to the ORDER BY inside OVER.
4. Filtering out the rows LAG needs

WHERE runs before LAG. If you write WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-02-01' in the same query, the January orders are gone and February's first order gets NULL instead of its real previous order. Calculate LAG in an inline view over the full range, then filter the dates in the outer query.
5. Expecting OVER (ORDER BY) to sort the output
The ORDER BY inside OVER only tells the function how to walk the rows. It does not promise the order of the final result. Always add a normal ORDER BY at the end of the query.
Performance tips

items.content: LAG and LEAD read the rows once after a sort, while a self join reads the table twice and matches rows. On large tables this is usually the bigger saving. In the plan you will typically see a WINDOW SORT step.
Several analytic functions with the same PARTITION BY and ORDER BY can share one sort. Keep the OVER clauses identical where you can.
An index on the partition and order columns, for example (customer_id, order_date), can let the optimizer read rows already sorted and skip the sort. Check the execution plan rather than assuming it.
Filter as early as is safe. Restricting to the customers you need in the WHERE clause shrinks the sort, as long as you do not remove rows that LAG must see (mistake 4).
The sort uses PGA memory and spills to the temporary tablespace when it does not fit, so very large partitions without filters can be slow.

data.text: See the related tutorial on reading Oracle explain plans to confirm what the optimizer chose for your query.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between LAG and LEAD in Oracle?

They take the same arguments and follow the same rules. LAG returns a value from a row before the current row, and LEAD returns a value from a row after it, in the order set by the ORDER BY inside OVER.
Can I use LAG without PARTITION BY?
Yes. PARTITION BY is optional. Without it, Oracle treats all rows of the result set as one group. The ORDER BY inside OVER is still required.
Can LAG be used in a WHERE clause?
No. Analytic functions are processed after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so Oracle raises ORA-30483. Compute LAG in a subquery or inline view, then filter in the outer query.
How do I get the previous non-null value in Oracle?
Use LAG(column) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY ...). It skips rows where the column is NULL and returns the nearest earlier non-null value.
How do I calculate the difference between the current and previous row?
Subtract LAG from the current value: amount - LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date). For dates, the result of subtracting two DATE values is the number of days between them.
Summary

items.content: LAG reads an earlier row, LEAD reads a later row, with no self join.
Always set ORDER BY inside OVER, and add a unique tie-breaker column.
Use PARTITION BY so values never cross from one customer or group to another.
Use the offset for rows further away and the default for rows that do not exist.
Use IGNORE NULLS to carry the last known value forward.
Filter on LAG or LEAD results in an outer query, never in the same WHERE clause.
Remember that the previous row is not always the previous month or day.

linkedin.post:
Comparing each row with the previous one in Oracle? You do not need a self join.

LAG reads an earlier row. LEAD reads a later row. The ORDER BY inside OVER decides what earlier means.

→ Change from last order: amount - LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)
→ Days to next order: LEAD(order_date) OVER (...) - order_date
→ Forget PARTITION BY and customer 2's first order reads customer 1's last order
→ LAG(price) IGNORE NULLS returns the last non-null value, handy for filling gaps
→ You cannot use LAG in WHERE (ORA-30483). Compute it in an inline view, filter outside
→ The default argument only applies when no row exists. NVL also replaces a real NULL

One more trap: LAG gives the previous row, not the previous month. A month with no sales simply disappears.
